newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks slide as payroll jitters mount.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks slide as payroll jitters mount.

text.p: Wall Street stocks skidded lower on Thursday as nervous investors braced for a payroll and wage report that many economists feel could signal whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates soon.
The Dow industrials fell 50 points to close unofficially at 5607, with most of the loss reflecting late sell programs.

"It was a combination of program selling and traders who got really nervous," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "It was one of those days where people thought it was better not to be too exposed."

An already uneasy market grew more tense early Thursday, when the U.S. Labor Department reported jobless claims last week fell by a greater-than-expected 15,000 after four straight weeks of increases.

Economists said the decline hinted at strong payroll data, and U.S. Treasuries fell after the figure was released. The benchmark 30-year bond fell 20/32 to yield 7.15 percent, a rate too high to let stocks make headway, analysts said.
"The last few days have shown stocks can't make upward progress when the long-bond yield is over seven percent," said UBS Securities Chief Investment Strategist Gail Dudack.
As is frequently the case, financial stocks bore the brunt of a sell-off focusing on interest rates. J.P. Morgan & Co fell 1-5/8 to 87, while BankAmerica Corp dropped 1-1/8 to 77-1/8.
Comments by two Federal Reserve officials sharpened the market's focus on Friday's report, although their remarks did little to signal the near-term outlook for Fed policy.
Speaking in Houston, Dallas Federal Reserve President Robert McTeer said the U.S. economy was "running hot," although he also noted that indicators he watched showed little sign of inflation.
Later, Fed Governor Janet Yellen said she expected U.S. demand growth to moderate to a more sustainable pace during the rest of 1996 and into 1997.
However, Yellen balanced that comment by observing that it remained "too soon to tell for sure whether wage pressures presented too much of an upside risk to the economy."
Stocks did pick up one vote of confidence from Fidelity Investments' Magellan fund. According to July data, Magellan added to its stock positions and reduced its holdings of both bonds and cash.
Fidelity said assets of the fund rose to $51.91 billion on September 4 from $50.97 billion at the end of July. One analyst who follows the fund said redemptions seem to be tapering off.
Eric Kobren, publisher of Fidelity Insight, said he estimated investors redeemed between $580 million and $600 million from the fund in August, "which was less than we saw in May, June or July."
American depositary shares in Russian companies fell in moderate U.S. trading after news that Russian President Boris Yeltsin had agreed to undergo heart surgery.
Templeton Russia Fund, the only closed-end fund on the NYSE that invests exclusively in Russian companies, fell 3/4 to 20-7/8.
A number of retail stocks struggled throughout the session after the release of weaker-than-expected monthly sales reports.

Gap Inc, which reported flat same-store sales versus a year ago, fell 4-7/8 to 29. The company said demin sales were weak last month, but it expected modest improvement in same store sales for the rest of the year.
Gap shares were the most active on the NYSE.
Kmart Corp fell 3/8 to 9-7/8. The company reported a one percent increase in August same-store sales and said its performance remains below plan.
Zilog Inc tumbled 8-3/8 to 15-1/2 after warning investors its third-quarter earnings per share would fall well short of second-quarter levels.
Campbell Soup Co surged 4-1/8 to 71-5/8 after announcing it would buy back $2.5 billion of stock and put into effect a consolidation and restructuring plan.
The Nasdaq Composite fell 18.16 to 1125.66.
The S&P 500 index fell 6.17 to 649.44.
(Figures official as of 1645 EDT/2045 GMT)
-- Wall Street desk, 212 859-1721
